common_name: Walberton Yellow Crocosmia (AGM Luminescent Golden-Yellow Montbretia)

planting.note: Plant corms about 4 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in groups in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun; Walberton Yellow was bred by David Tristram and, after RHS Wisley trials, received the Award of Garden Merit for its exceptionally clean, luminous yellow color and strong constitution.

directions: Plant corms in moderately fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Walberton Yellow bears strong, arching stems carrying large, luminescent golden-yellow tubular flowers from mid to late summer, a purer and more sun-bright yellow than most older yellow crocosmia selections, and one of a trio of Tristram-bred crocosmias singled out from ninety-seven trial varieties at RHS Garden Wisley for the Award of Garden Merit. It builds into substantial upright clumps within two to three seasons and holds up well without staking. Water during dry spells, since inadequate moisture noticeably reduces flowering, and lift or mulch heavily where winters are severe.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Mistral is a vigorous, tall-growing crocosmia whose bright red flowers open from a contrasting yellow throat.

directions: Plant corms in fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Mistral sends up narrow, pleated, erect foliage topped by tall sprays of bright red flowers tinged with fiery orange, each bloom opening from a yellowish throat, on stems reaching a meter in height by mid to late summer. It is a notably vigorous grower that multiplies rapidly by cormlets and can crowd out slower neighbors if left undivided, so lift and separate congested clumps every three to four years in spring. In colder gardens, shelter it from drying winter winds and apply a thick, dry mulch over the corms.

common_name: His Majesty Crocosmia (Giant Dark Orange Bicolor Montbretia)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; His Majesty is prized for producing some of the largest individual flowers of any crocosmia cultivar, up to 4 inches across.

directions: Plant corms in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade. His Majesty produces exceptionally large, star-shaped flowers opening bright yellow in the throat and deepening to dark orange at the petal edges, held on gently arching, sturdy stems from midsummer into autumn, with individual blooms notably bigger than those of most named crocosmia cultivars. Its bold bicolor flowers make a strong focal point in a hot-colored border and are long-lasting when cut. Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, and mulch over the corms for winter protection at the colder end of its hardiness range.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Zeal Tan is a compact, dark-stemmed selection and one of the latest crocosmia cultivars to bloom, flowering into early autumn.

directions: Plant corms in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Zeal Tan is a compact, lower-growing crocosmia with deep olive and chocolate-tinted stems and foliage that set off its outward-facing, reddish-scarlet flowers, each centered with a small sunny-yellow eye and widely spaced, gently recurving petals, opening from midsummer well into early autumn — later than most other named cultivars. Its dark, tan-tinted coloring and shorter stature make it useful toward the front of a hot border or in containers. Divide crowded clumps every few years in early spring to sustain vigorous late bloom, and mulch over the corms where winters are cold.

common_name: Coleton Fishacre Crocosmia (Vigorous Apricot-Yellow Bronze-Foliage Montbretia)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Coleton Fishacre is a more vigorous, sturdier-stemmed improvement on the older 'Solfatare', named for the National Trust garden in Devon where it was selected.

directions: Plant corms in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Coleton Fishacre carries rich golden apricot-yellow tubular flowers above cool, grey-green, coppery-bronze pleated foliage on stocky, self-supporting stems, an improvement on the similar but less robust 'Solfatare' that rarely needs staking. It forms tidy, reliably hardy clumps that build steadily without becoming invasive, making it well suited to cottage-style borders where its warm flowers pair nicely with its smoky foliage. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, and give it a protective mulch over winter in the colder parts of its range.

common_name: Rowallane Yellow Crocosmia (AGM Chrome-Yellow Giant Montbretia)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun; Rowallane Yellow is a chrome-yellow selection of the bold species Crocosmia masoniorum, originating at the National Trust's Rowallane Garden in Northern Ireland and holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant corms in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun. Rowallane Yellow forms an erect clump of narrow, pleated, sword-shaped leaves and arching, single-sided spikes of clear chrome-yellow flowers held outward-facing in a showy taper, a large-flowered selection that stands out for its unusually pure, saturated yellow among the mostly orange and red masoniorum-type crocosmias. It flowers most heavily in full sun and needs consistently full light to perform to its potential, unlike some crocosmias that tolerate part shade. Lift and divide congested clumps in early spring as growth resumes to keep it flowering strongly, and mulch the corms over winter in colder zones.
